paras: The whitecapping and Black flight from Amite County, Mississippi, was the departure of Black farm laborers and tenants from Amite County around the turn of 1903, under night raids and threats by bands of white men whom Mississippi papers called whitecappers. Dispatches from New Orleans and Mobile reported that Black residents were leaving "in droves," mostly at night, despite a recent "compromise agreement." The story ran as a wire brief in papers from New York to North Dakota and Vermont, and the Cleveland Gazette reprinted it and later condemned the whitecaps in an editorial.

In late December 1902 a Jackson dispatch to the Hattiesburg Daily Progress said the trouble with whitecappers in Franklin, Amite, Pike and Lincoln counties had reached "a most acute stage." According to that report, the "negro question" was the main issue, and in Amite the movement aimed "to prevent negroes from owning farms or tenanting the lands of non-resident owners." The same dispatch said the Amite whitecappers, known as the "Farmer's Club," had been called to meet on Saturday, January 3. On January 3 the Chicago Broad Ax, a Black weekly, reported that Governor Longino had ordered the whitecaps of Amite and Franklin counties to disperse and offered a $50 reward for the arrest and conviction of each member.

A New Orleans dispatch dated January 1 reported that, in spite of the compromise, Black residents of Amite County remained "terror-stricken by lawless bands" and were leaving, mostly at night and by train from way stations. A Mobile dispatch of January 3 described them as "negro laborers" fleeing "lawless bands of white men" and placed the center of the disturbance between Gloster and Liberty. Both dispatches said white farmers and businessmen were sleeping on their plantations with shotguns, vowing to kill any night raider who molested their tenants.

On January 6 the Hattiesburg Daily Progress reported that night riders had left a notice at the home of B. F. Binn in Amite County, ordering him to leave with all his laborers or have his houses burned. The paper added that county officers seeking re-election held back for fear of losing the votes of "the lawless element," as Black residents left "in droves." None of these reports describes anyone killed or injured in connection with the departures.

Later in January, U.S. deputy marshals arrested Z. T. Smith, W. T. Smith, Tom Way and Ted Huff in Amite County on a federal charge of conspiring to intimidate homesteaders. After waiving examination before a U.S. commissioner at Vicksburg, the four were held in the Jackson jail under bonds of $2,000 each. In mid-February the Greenville Times quoted the Natchez Bulletin as saying that no one would go on their bonds and that they would likely stay in jail until trial in federal court, but no report of the trial's outcome was found.
In March the Cleveland Gazette reported that Black families from Amite and the lower counties of Mississippi were moving to the Delta, with hundreds passing through Vicksburg.

Outside Mississippi the white press ran the story as a wire brief: the Sun of New York headed it "Terrorized Negroes Still Leaving Louisiana," misplacing the county, and the Bismarck Daily Tribune "Terror for Negroes." The St. Johnsbury Caledonian reduced the story to a single line in its weekly news digest under Saturday, January 3.

Mississippi papers treated the bands as a threat to law and order, calling them "the lawless element," and the Natchez Bulletin, as quoted in Greenville, said the arrested men had enjoyed "terrorizing the colored labor" and that their jailing was "exactly right."

Among Black papers, the Cleveland Gazette reprinted the New Orleans wire on January 10 as "Still Leaving Louisiana," changing "the negroes" to "our people" and inserting "(white)" after "night raider." Its March 7 editorial, "Whitecaps Persecuting and Driving Out," portrayed the people driven off as thrifty, prosperous farmers, said it was "the better class of Afro-Americans" who were fleeing, and mocked the South as "the best(?) friend of the Negro." The Broad Ax gave the story a single sentence in a column of local and political notes, crediting the governor with opening "a fierce warfare on the white-caps."

accounts.label: Mobile dispatch
accounts.gist: Black laborers fleeing lawless bands of white men; the center of trouble is between Gloster and Liberty, and planters may seek state aid.

accounts.label: Jackson correspondent (Hattiesburg Daily Progress)
accounts.gist: Whitecapper bands in four counties aim to keep Black residents from owning or renting land; night riders threaten employers; officers hold back for political reasons.

accounts.label: Cleveland Gazette editorial
accounts.gist: Whitecaps are driving thrifty, prosperous Black farmers from Amite and lower counties; the South tolerates the outrages.

framing.detail: Northern papers ran the wire as a brief: 'Terrorized Negroes Still Leaving Louisiana' (Sun), 'Terror for Negroes' (Bismarck), a one-line digest item (St. Johnsbury).
Mississippi papers called the bands 'the lawless element' and the Natchez Bulletin said jailing the whitecappers was 'exactly right'.
Cleveland Gazette reprinted the wire as 'our people' and '(white)' night raiders, then ran the editorial 'Whitecaps Persecuting and Driving Out'.
Broad Ax noted the governor's 'fierce warfare on the white-caps' in a column item.

conflicts.note: The Louisiana headlines follow the New Orleans dateline; the text names Amite County, which the Mobile dispatch and Mississippi papers place in Mississippi.
